Stanger says she always writes her own first drafts and outlines her own argument before involving AI.
Stanger says humans are best at judging what good writing is, so AI cannot replace showing writing to another human.
Stanger says the main danger of AI lies in the concentration of power rather than in the technology itself.
Stanger says AI is potentially very dangerous and people must keep thinking for themselves and teach students to do so.
Reading, science and math performance among 15-year-olds declined globally in the 2025 PISA.
Students in Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Singapore were among the top performers in the 2025 PISA.
Japan, South Korea, Macao and Taiwan were also in the top 10 across all three PISA subjects.
US secondary students' reading scores in PISA fell close to 25-year lows.
China's PISA data is criticised because only four wealthy eastern coastal provinces and cities submitted scores.
China has surpassed the US in published scientific reports and in research spending.
Andreas Schleicher says the most troubling trend is the decline in skills for evaluating information, connecting multiple sources and thinking critically about reading.
The proportion of 'hasty readers' who rush through texts and answer incorrectly nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025.
Fewer than 10% of students in China, Japan and South Korea reported peers being distracted by digital devices in science lessons, versus a 28% global average.
The share of OECD students below baseline PISA performance rose to 20% in 2025 from 16% in 2022.
A Stanford study cited in the PISA report estimates that basic aptitude for all 15-year-old Americans could add over $40 trillion to the US economy over their working lives.
Singapore uses technology in classrooms but emphasizes reading comprehension early on.
PISA found that students using AI moderately (about monthly to once or twice weekly) had higher average science scores than both rare and near-daily users.
Students who used AI weekly to summarize reading or research performed about the same as AI nonusers after accounting for socioeconomic status.
The OECD says the relationship between AI use and science performance may reflect who adopts AI and how, rather than a negative impact of AI.
86% of students across OECD countries used AI chatbots for at least one schoolwork purpose.
Students who do not use AI chatbots for schoolwork generally score higher than those who do.
About one in five students use AI almost every day and tend to score lower in science than non-users, accounting for socioeconomic status.
Reading, mathematics and science scores have dropped since 2003, so lower scores are not all due to AI.
Weaker critical reading ability makes it harder for students to recognize incomplete or incorrect AI answers, and heavy reliance on AI reduces chances to develop those skills.
Nearly three in four K-12 teachers believe AI has bigger implications for education than the internet or computers.

Six in 10 polled teachers have used AI themselves for work tasks.

Special education teacher Ellie Rodriguez says AI can help students with disabilities complete assignments they otherwise could not.
A study of about 27,000 students in China found homework scores rose 18% after adopting generative AI while time per assignment fell about 30%.
The same students' scores on monthly closed-book exams without AI fell 20% within six months of adopting generative AI.
The OECD's Digital Education Outlook 2026 found that where generative AI is neither built to teach nor used under structure, outsourcing tasks improves performance without real learning gains.
In a survey of 7,000 European students aged 12–17, 31% said they use AI to provide complete solutions to tasks.
In the HEPI/Kortext survey, 49% of UK undergraduates believe AI has improved their student experience.
Georgia Tech professors are building AI tutor agents and replacing long essays with in-class discussion in response to AI.
